scene.testo: It is 6 AM, 250 miles above Earth, and you are traveling at 17,500 miles per hour. Your bed is a sleeping bag strapped to a wall. You have no up, no down, and no pillow. Open your eyes. The day begins.

While you slept, the station circled the planet about three times. That is how fast it moves. Outside your window, the sun has already risen and set more than once. Your night was only about eight hours long. Orbit does not care.

So what do astronauts really do at night on the space station? Not what you imagine. There is no night at all, not the kind you know. And the truth about sleeping up here is stranger, louder, and more carefully planned than anyone expects.

Here is the first shock. The International Space Station orbits Earth about every 90 minutes. That means the crew sees about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day. Think about that. Sixteen dawns before you finish a normal 24-hour day.

So the crew cannot trust the sun. If they did, their bodies would never know when to sleep. Instead, NASA runs the station on a clock. The station uses Greenwich Mean Time, the time in London, no matter where the crew is flying.

Why London time? Because the crew comes from many countries, and the ground teams sit in many time zones. One shared clock keeps everyone in step. Lights go out on schedule, and the crew sleeps about eight hours a night, planned like a mission task.

Now imagine the end of your workday. You have been up since 6 AM. You have run experiments, fixed equipment, and exercised. Your body wants rest. But first, there are chores, and the biggest one is dinner. Let me show you how it works.

Dinner is packaged food. Much of it is sealed in pouches. Some is dehydrated, so you add water through a needle, then squeeze and knead. Other items come ready to eat. Nothing is served on a regular plate. Plates would simply float away.

Food is held down with Velcro and clips. Utensils stick to trays. The crew eats together when possible, gathered around a table in the Russian segment or the American side. Meals are social events, and they matter for morale far from home.

Crumbs are a real problem. In microgravity, a loose crumb drifts, and it can be inhaled or clog equipment. So bread is avoided. NASA has long favored tortillas instead. They hold together and leave almost no mess in the air.

Drinks come in sealed pouches with straws. You cannot pour anything. A drop of liquid does not fall. It forms a wobbling sphere and floats until it sticks to something. Astronauts have even filmed themselves chasing water bubbles through the air.

After dinner, there is cleanup, then personal time. And here is something you can try to picture. Washing yourself with no shower. Water does not run down a body in orbit. It clings. So astronauts clean up with a different method.

They use rinseless soap and wet towels. Squeeze a little water onto a cloth and wipe down. Hair is washed with no-rinse shampoo, then toweled. Every drop is collected, because on the station, water is recycled and nothing is wasted.

That recycling is remarkable. The station reclaims water from sweat, breath moisture, and even urine, then purifies it for drinking. NASA has reported that its recovery system can reach about 98 percent of the water the crew uses.

Teeth are brushed with regular toothpaste. But there is no sink to spit into. Astronauts swallow it, or spit into a towel. It is one of those small things that sounds gross on Earth and feels perfectly normal in orbit.

Now comes a job you may not expect. Exercise. Astronauts work out about two hours every day, and not only in the morning. Floating bodies lose muscle and bone, so the crew trains hard to push back against that slow loss.

There is a treadmill with a harness that pulls you down against the belt. There is a bike, and there is a resistance machine that uses vacuum cylinders instead of weights. Weights would be pointless. Everything weighs almost nothing up here.

Why the effort? NASA research shows astronauts can lose bone density at a rate of up to about 1 percent per month without countermeasures. Exercise and diet reduce that loss. It is a daily fight against what weightlessness does to a body.

Now it is evening. Some astronauts call family on video. Some read. Some look out the window for hours. The station has a large viewing dome called the Cupola, with seven windows. It is the favorite spot for watching Earth glide past.

From the Cupola, you can see cities glowing at night. Lightning flashes inside storms. The aurora ripples green across the poles. And all of it passes beneath you at 17,500 miles per hour, so every view is gone in minutes.

Astronauts have said in interviews that this is when the planet feels most real. A thin blue line of atmosphere. No borders drawn on the ground. Many describe a lasting change in how they see Earth. They call it the overview effect.

Others use free time to take photos. Crews have shared thousands of pictures from orbit with the public. A camera strapped to a wrist or a wall, a long lens, and patience. A single clear night over a city can be a prize.

There is also music, movies, and games. Crews have played instruments aboard the station. Some have a tablet with downloaded films. Some video chat with friends. The goal is simple. Keep the mind rested, because a tired mind makes expensive mistakes.

Now it is bedtime. Where do you actually sleep? Not on a mattress. Each astronaut has a small private cabin about the size of a phone booth, or a sleeping bag clipped to a wall in another module. Walls, floor, or ceiling, it makes no difference.

The sleeping bag is tied down, because if it were not, you would drift all night and bump into equipment. Your arms float up in front of you, which feels odd at first. Many astronauts tuck them inside the bag to feel secure.

There is no pillow in the usual sense. In weightlessness, your head does not press into anything. Some astronauts report feeling their neck relax and their head tilt forward. A few use a strap or a small cushion to hold position.

The cabin has a light, a laptop, a few personal items, and a vent. That vent matters more than you think. On Earth, warm air rises and carries your exhaled breath away. In orbit, it does not. So the fans must never stop.

Without airflow, carbon dioxide can pool around a sleeper's face. It forms an invisible bubble of stale air. That can cause headaches, drowsiness, and worse. So fans run all night, and sensors watch the air. Silence in a cabin would be a warning.
scene.q: station air quality carbon dioxide monitor

scene.testo: And those fans are loud. The station is never quiet. Pumps, fans, and cooling loops hum around the clock. Astronauts have said in interviews that the noise is constant, and many sleep with earplugs. Peace and quiet is not part of the design.

Many also wear eye masks, because the Sun rises every 90 minutes. Even with the shades closed, flashes of light can leak in. Some astronauts have reported seeing odd flashes of light with their eyes closed, caused by cosmic rays.

Yes, cosmic rays. Particles from space pass through the station and sometimes through an astronaut's eyes. NASA has documented these light flashes in crews since the Apollo era. The cause is believed to be radiation striking the retina.

Temperature is another factor. The station keeps its cabin air around room temperature, roughly 70°F. Outside, though, it is brutal. Sunlit surfaces can reach about +250°F, while shaded surfaces drop to about -250°F. Only a thin wall separates you from that.

That is 250 degrees above and below zero Fahrenheit, swinging every 45 minutes or so as the station passes from sunlight into Earth's shadow. The station is built to survive those cycles for years. Thermal control systems move heat around constantly.

The station is also huge. Its pressurized space is roughly the volume of a six-bedroom house, and the full structure spans about the length of an American football field, around 357 feet including its solar arrays. Yet crews live in tight quarters.

Even while you sleep, the station is working. Mission controllers in Houston and Moscow watch the systems around the clock. Flight controllers work in shifts. Someone is always monitoring air, power, temperature, and pressure while the crew rests.

If an alarm sounds, the crew wakes up. There are alarms for fire, rapid pressure loss, and toxic air. Crews train for these emergencies on the ground and in orbit. At night, a sleeping astronaut must be ready in seconds.

There are also tiny chunks of space debris to worry about. The station can maneuver to dodge tracked objects. Sometimes the crew shelters in their return spacecraft as a precaution while a close pass is checked. It has happened, and it is documented.

Still, most nights are calm. Lights dim. Voices fade. The hum continues. The station glides over oceans and continents while the crew sleeps. Below, billions of people are doing the same, and none of them can feel the speed above them.

Here is how this compares with your night at home. You lie on a soft mattress, feel the pull of gravity, and hear a quiet room. An astronaut floats in a bag, hears constant fans, and circles the planet. Both of you are simply trying to rest.

Sleep itself is a challenge up there. Studies of astronauts show they often sleep less than on Earth, commonly around six hours rather than the scheduled eight. Light, noise, and a busy schedule all play a part. NASA tracks this closely.

To help, crews use special lighting. Some station lights can shift color, with bluer light for alertness and warmer light before bed. The idea comes from research on circadian rhythms, our internal body clock. It is science used to protect rest.

Now the strangest detail. Your body changes while you sleep up there. Without gravity pulling fluids downward, they shift toward your head. Faces look puffy. Many astronauts feel congested. Some wake up with a stuffy nose, as if they had a cold.

And here is the most surprising part. Astronauts often say they dream about falling, floating, and flying, and some report dreams where gravity suddenly returns. Their accounts are personal and vary. But the idea fits one truth. Even in sleep, the mind misses home.

So when you tuck in tonight, remember this. Somewhere above you, 250 miles up, a person is clipped to a wall, wearing earplugs, listening to fans, while sixteen sunrises roll by. Sleep is something they must plan, protect, and truly earn.
